- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.5) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly.
- When sentiment turns negative or mixed (≤0.5), model often overcorrects or underestimates; increase forecast if recent price is falling, or adjust downward if sentiment is bearish.
- After sharp price spikes, model frequently overshoots in the next few days; apply a “cool-down” correction by reducing forecast by 5–10% for the following 3–5 days.
- If model forecast is significantly above true outcome (e.g., >10% deviation) and sentiment is neutral or bearish, assume mean reversion; adjust forecast toward historical mean or recent 7-day average.
- For 30-day horizon, model often fails to capture short-term volatility; if sentiment is volatile or recent price moved sharply, reduce forecast confidence and apply a ±3–5% buffer.
- When sentiment history shows repeated negative spikes followed by recovery, model tends to overreact; apply a “lag correction” — delay forecast peak by 1–2 days if sentiment is bullish but price is flat or declining.
